title: A new front door for WFRC Analytics
text:
WFRC Analytics works across many repositories, apps and reports. This site is the front door to all of it.

Explore lists the live apps and maps, such as the commute flow explorers and the housing access calculator.
Models explains the Travel Demand, Real-Estate Market and Bike Demand models, with current releases and links to full documentation.
Reports & methods collects the estimation, calibration and validation write-ups behind the models.
Data and Code list datasets and every repository, with a clear Internal label on those that need WFRC GitHub access.

The lists are generated from a single catalog, so new tools appear here without hand-editing pages. Spotted something missing or wrong? Tell us through the contact page.

title: About WFRC Analytics
text:
The Wasatch Front Regional Council (WFRC) is the Metropolitan Planning Organization for the Salt Lake and Ogden-Layton urban areas. It serves six counties: Box Elder, Davis, Morgan, Salt Lake, Tooele and Weber.
WFRC’s mission is to build consensus and enhance quality of life by developing and implementing visions and plans for a well-functioning multi-modal transportation system, livable communities, a strong economy, and a healthy environment.
The Analytics team builds the data, models and tools that give those plans a quantitative foundation.

title: Travel Demand Model
text:
Reproducible runs and calibration
Two repositories apply the model in a traceable, repeatable way:

TDM run results publishes experiment results, such as sensitivity tests, project alternatives and forecasting scenarios. Each run records exactly which model version and settings produced it.
TDM calibration reports show each calibration iteration. Calibration is tied to a pinned model version so that results can be reproduced.

The calibration dashboard summarizes calibration results by scenario, and the vizTool (source) helps explore model results through maps and charts.

title: Get the model
text:
Getting the Travel Demand Model


1. Read the release letter
Everyone who uses the model agrees to the release letter. In short:

You are responsible for how you apply the model and interpret its results.
Contact WFRC or MAG staff before applying it, especially a new release, to discuss your planned use, method and whether you have the current version. Staff can revoke access if this is skipped.
If you modify the model, keep a record of the changes and say so when you share results.
Please give feedback on how the model performs, and ask for enhancements.
Do not pass the model on. Send others to request it from WFRC or MAG, so they get the current version and join the Model User Group email list.

The full letter is at the top of the model repository’s page, which you can read once you have access.


2. Ask for access
Email WFRC. WFRC’s page says to contact the data scientist who handles model requests:

 Suzie Swim, WFRC Data Scientist: suzie.swim@wfrc.utah.gov

Tell them who you are, what you plan to use the model for, and your GitHub username. WFRC and MAG (which co-develops the model) both support model users. If you are unsure whom to write to, use the contact page.
You will also need a GitHub account. The model lives in a private repository, so WFRC grants access to it. The repository’s documentation says users must have a GitHub account and may lose repository access if they do not follow the release letter.


3. Download a release
Once you have access, open the model repository’s Releases page and choose a version. Under Assets, download Source code. You can instead fork the repository and clone it to your computer.
Versions listed there: 10.0.0 (beta), 9.2.0, 9.1.1, 9.1.0, 9.0.2, 9.0.1, 9.0.0 and 8.3.2. For a study that must follow adopted plans, use the current release (9.2.0) unless WFRC staff advise otherwise.


4. Read the documentation
Documentation for every version is on the WFRC documentation site: for example, version 9.2.0 has a What’s New document and a Model Validation Report. Version 10 documentation is under development.
See the release table for the version history and dates.


5. Ask questions
The repository has two channels. Use the right one so the team can respond quickly:

Discussions for general questions, ideas and troubleshooting.
Issues for actionable items such as bug fixes and feature requests.

For anything else, email WFRC or MAG staff directly.


What is in the model
WFRC describes it as a modified four-step, trip-based model with a travel-time feedback loop. It forecasts traffic volumes and transit ridership through 2050. The release includes networks for base, existing and future years, reflecting funded Transportation Improvement Program projects and the adopted Regional Transportation Plans (both fiscally constrained and needs-based), with matching socioeconomic projections in the WFRC area.

title: Bike Demand Model
text: The model builds on the micromobility toolset from RSG, applied to Utah data. It estimates how many bicycle trips happen between small zones and which parts of the bike network they use.

title: Bike Demand Model
text:
How it works





flowchart LR
  A[Convert<br/>network] --> C[Trip<br/>generation]
  B[Create<br/>microzones] --> C
  C --> D[Trip<br/>distribution] --> E[Trip<br/>assignment] --> F[Post-process<br/>outputs]







Convert the network. Prepares the bike network for the model.
Create microzones. Builds the small zones the model works in (see below).
Run the bike demand model. Trip generation, trip distribution and trip assignment.
Post-process outputs. Produces monthly bike volume across links, microzone-to-microzone trip summaries and microzone centroid nodes, used for quality checks.

title: Bike Demand Model
text:
Microzones
Microzones, or micro analysis zones (MAZ), are smaller than the traffic analysis zones used by the Travel Demand Model. They are typically about the size of a census block and group areas with similar land use, such as residential, commercial, industrial, education, parks and open space. They also follow Wasatch Choice Centers, and buildings within a microzone tend to share similar points of access to the network. This finer scale suits bicycle travel, where short trips matter.

title: Bike Demand Model
text:
Running the model
The model needs at least 32 GB of RAM and Python 3.
pip install git+https://github.com/rsginc/micromobility_toolset
python Create_Microzones.py        # if microzone data is needed
python Convert_MM_Network.py       # if network data is needed
python utah_bike_demand_model.py   # run the full model
Add --name generate_demand or --name assign_demand to run one step, or --sample 100 to run only the first 100 microzones. Outputs are saved in the repository’s logs folder. See the full instructions.

text: Where will Utahns live and work in the future? REMM projects future residential and employment-related development using the UrbanSim modeling platform. WFRC runs a modified version of UrbanSim.

title: Real-Estate Market Model
text:
What it does
REMM considers how much land is available and how profitable new development and redevelopment would be. It is first calibrated to reproduce the base year of the adopted Regional Transportation Plan, currently 2023. It then simulates development forward in time to produce household and job projections.

title: Real-Estate Market Model
text:
What goes in
The model draws on the best available regional sources:

A region-wide parcel land use and valuation database
An inventory of local government general plans
The results of a multi-year scenario-based visioning exercise
A synthesized household population dataset for the model’s base year, built from Census data
Address-geocoded employment totals from the Utah Department of Workforce Services (DWS)
County-level employment and population control totals from the Kem C. Gardner Policy Institute at the University of Utah
Input from public and private sector expert advisors
“Physical constraint” map layers showing where development is prohibited or impractical because of steep terrain, wetlands, mining, or public lands
